title: Salt Analysis (Class XII): One Cation, One Anion
objective: Apply the same systematic scheme as XI-CHE-F01, with the anion list extended to include oxalate
Distinguish oxalate from carbonate, since both are salts of a weak acid that can effervesce or react with acid depending on conditions
Confirm oxalate specifically by its decolourisation of warm, acidified KMnO4
Combine cation and anion evidence to state the identity of the given salt

theory.statement: The Class XII salt-analysis scheme repeats the systematic approach of Class XI (preliminary tests narrowing the field, confirmatory tests settling it) but with oxalate, C2O4^2-, added to the anions that must be considered — a salt of a weak diprotic acid that, unlike carbonate, does NOT effervesce with dilute acid at room temperature but does reduce warm acidified permanganate.
theory.derivationNote: Because oxalate does not effervesce with dilute acid, it can initially be mistaken for one of the 'unreactive' anions (sulphate, chloride, nitrate) at the preliminary stage. Its confirmatory test — decolourising a few drops of dilute, acidified KMnO4 on warming — is unambiguous and ties this experiment back to the redox titrations of Section J.
keyEquations: CO3^2- + 2H+ → H2O + CO2 (carbonate effervesces; oxalate does not, at room temperature)

apparatus.name: Given salt
apparatus.why: The sample whose cation and anion are to be identified

apparatus.name: Dilute hydrochloric/sulphuric acid
apparatus.why: Preliminary test for a volatile anion (carbonate); oxalate gives no effervescence here

apparatus.name: Dilute, acidified KMnO4
apparatus.why: Confirmatory test for oxalate, which decolourises it on warming

apparatus.name: Silver nitrate, barium chloride solutions
apparatus.why: Confirmatory reagents for halide and sulphate respectively

procedure.text: Note the colour and physical form of the salt.
Add dilute acid; note whether effervescence occurs (carbonate) or not (oxalate/sulphate/chloride/nitrate all possible if no gas).
If no effervescence, test a fresh portion by warming with a few drops of dilute, acidified KMnO4 to check for oxalate.
Perform the flame test and the NaOH/NH4OH precipitation tests to narrow the cation.
Perform the specific confirmatory test(s) for both the cation and the anion.
State the identity of the salt, with evidence for both ions.

steps: Run preliminary tests, checking specifically for oxalate's non-effervescence
Confirm oxalate (if suspected) with warm acidified KMnO4
State the cation and anion with supporting evidence

expectedResult.quantity: Number of salts correctly identified (cation + anion), Class XII extended list
expectedResult.statement: The extended Class XII scheme correctly distinguishes oxalate from the other 'non-effervescing' anions by its specific reaction with warm, acidified permanganate — the same redox chemistry standardised quantitatively in Section J.

safety: Some reagents (concentrated acids, ammonia, KMnO4) are corrosive/irritating — work in a ventilated space.
Barium and lead salts are toxic — wash hands after handling.
sourcesOfError: Assuming any anion that doesn't effervesce with acid must be sulphate or chloride, without testing for oxalate specifically.
Using cold rather than warm KMnO4 for the oxalate test, which reacts too slowly cold to give a clear result.
Concluding from a single test rather than combining several lines of evidence.

viva.question: How would you distinguish a carbonate from an oxalate salt, given that both are salts of weak acids?
viva.expectedConcept: Carbonate effervesces readily with dilute acid at room temperature, releasing CO2 that turns lime water milky. Oxalate does NOT effervesce with dilute acid under these conditions; it is instead confirmed by its ability to decolourise warm, acidified potassium permanganate — a redox reaction, not an acid-base one.
viva.answerLogic: Different confirmatory chemistry: acid-base gas test vs. redox decolourisation.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting oxalate to effervesce with dilute acid the way carbonate does.

viva.question: Why must the KMnO4 used to test for oxalate be both acidified AND warmed?
viva.expectedConcept: Acidification ensures MnO4- is reduced cleanly to Mn2+ (n-factor 5) rather than to MnO2, and warming speeds up the otherwise slow, autocatalysed oxalate/permanganate reaction so the decolourisation is clear within a reasonable time.
viva.answerLogic: Both conditions matter for a clean, timely confirmatory result.
viva.commonMisconception: Testing with neutral or cold KMnO4 and getting an ambiguous, slow result.

viva.question: This confirmatory oxalate test uses the same reaction as which quantitative experiment in the syllabus?
viva.expectedConcept: The same MnO4-/oxalate redox reaction used here qualitatively is titrated quantitatively in XII-CHE-J01, to standardise a KMnO4 solution against standard oxalic acid.
viva.answerLogic: Connects qualitative confirmatory chemistry to the quantitative titration.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating the two experiments as chemically unrelated.

preLab.question: Which anion does NOT effervesce with dilute acid but IS confirmed by decolourising warm acidified KMnO4?
preLab.feedback: Oxalate is unreactive with dilute acid at room temperature but reduces warm acidified permanganate, decolourising it.

duringLab.question: Run at least four different tests before concluding.

postLab.question: The oxalate confirmatory test relies on:
postLab.feedback: Oxalate reduces warm, acidified MnO4- to Mn2+, decolourising the purple permanganate — a redox, not acid-base, confirmatory test.

scientificValidation.formula: Systematic analysis; oxalate confirmed by MnO4- redox decolourisation
assumptions: One cation and one anion present, from the extended syllabus list
edgeCases: Oxalate does not effervesce with dilute acid, unlike carbonate
expectedBehaviour: Correct systematic testing identifies both ions, including oxalate via its redox behaviour
